abstract: Evolution of active sites is a common fact, which originates from entropy gains or enthalpy lost that effectively regulates the selectivities and rates during catalysis, however, is very difficult to probe. In this work, a PdCu organic precursor was synthesized and dispersed well on SiO2 support by impregnation method (c.a. Pd1Cu1/SiO2). Within the initial stage of phenylacetylene hydrogenation, Pd1Cu1/SiO2 showed severe overhydrogenation. Consequently, Pd species were carburized to PdCuCx ensembles and facilitated the styrene formation significantly (>99% conv., >98% selec.). Interestingly, the activation process was highly dependent on the type and concentration of the reactant gas, in which the increase of alkyne concentration promoted the evolution of active sites (i.e. carbonization of Pd) and improved styrene formation, whereas the promotion of hydrogen stabilized palladium hydride and hindered carbonization process, which led to the overhydrogenation. These findings were well evidenced by catalytic performance evaluation and relative characterizations, i.e. quasi-in situ XPS and HRTEM etc. Clearly, the dynamics of PdCuCx ensemble generation were significantly correlated to the concentrations of the alkyne and hydrogen, which could modify the selective hydrogenation behaviour greatly.

abstract: Catalytic chain-growth of light oxygenates is a promising pathway for bio-oil valorisation. In this work, the C–C coupling of acetone on TiO 2 was investigated by activity tests, thermodynamic calculations and kinetic analysis. Conversion trends and product yields at varying operating conditions revealed a chain-growth reaction scheme composed of consecutive and parallel routes. Self and cross condensation reactions led to mesityl oxide as primary C 6 product, and two cyclic C 9 compounds, mesitylene and isophorone. C 4 , C 7 and C 10 olefins were produced by competitive β-scission reactions. Increasing temperature favoured the production of C 9 species and olefins, and the nearly constant acetone conversion observed at varying acetone concentration indicated global first-order kinetics. The effect of space velocity showed that mesityl oxide is an intermediate product, while mesitylene is a terminal product. Thermodynamic properties ( Δ H r , j 0 , Δ G r , j 0 ) and equilibrium constants were calculated for the entire set of reactions, and the K eq of the primary C 3 → C 6 step turned out to be markedly lower than those of other reactions. In contrast, the formation of mesitylene was thermodynamically favoured across the investigated temperature range. Reaction rates, apparent rate constants and activation energies of single reactions were calculated, demonstrating an overall kinetic limitation imposed by the primary condensation step, likely arising from the accumulation of heavy reaction intermediates/products in the catalytic pores, as indicated by the characterization of unloaded catalyst. This work proves the potential of TiO 2 to produce C 7+ hydrocarbons and identifies the kinetic and thermodynamic drivers that govern acetone condensation, key insights for catalyst and process optimization.

abstract: Pt-MoO x /TiO 2 catalysts are highly efficient for the hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) of tetrahydrofuran-2,5-dicarboxylic acid (THFDCA) to adipic acid (AA), while suppressing carboxyl reduction and decarboxylation/decarbonylation. However, the active site(s) governing HDO selectivity remains unclear. Here, surface characterizations, chemical probe analysis, spectroscopy, and kinetic studies were combined to investigate the formation, evolution, and reactivity of surface Pt, isolated MoO x , and Pt-MoO x interfacial sites during THFDCA conversion to AA. The Mo loading was systematically varied (Mo:Pt = 0:1 to 10:1 M ratio) to evaluate the progressive formation of active centers and control the extent of Pt decoration by MoO x . Pt/MoO 3 systems, where yields of up to 79% were obtained, served as references to evaluate the behavior of Pt-MoO x interfacial sites. Results from XRD, IR spectroscopy, O 2 -pulse chemisorption, HR-STEM, and EDS mapping demonstrated that Mo preferentially deposits on TiO 2 , forming highly dispersed MoO x species at sub-monolayer (Mo:Pt ≤ 2:1) and MoO 3 domains near monolayer (Mo:Pt ≥ 5:1) coverages. CO-FTIR, CO-pulse chemisorption, and H 2 -TPR showed that Mo progressively decorates neighboring Pt nanoparticles as its concentration increases, forming Pt-MoO x interfacial sites. Pt-MoO x /TiO 2 catalysts with Mo:Pt ≥ 5:1 exhibited local catalytic environments comparable to those of Pt/MoO 3 , consistent with their similar product distribution. Kinetic and catalytic analyses ultimately revealed a site-dependent reaction network in which THFDCA ring-opening occur on Pt-TiO 2 and Pt-MoO x ensembles, whereas HDO of 2-hydroxyadipic acid (2-HAA) to AA is only promoted at Pt-MoO x interfaces by BAS, likely through acid-catalyzed dehydration. The findings in this work provide mechanistic insights and design principles for selective biomass-upgrading catalysts.

title: Metal- and additive-free cascade synthesis of diarylamines from biomass-derived feedstocks catalyzed by oxidized carbon
abstract: Diarylamines are critical substructures in various pharmaceuticals and functional molecules. However, their conventional synthesis predominantly depends on transition-metal catalysis, which often involves toxic, non-renewable feedstocks and leads to significant chemical waste generation. In this work, a novel, metal- and additive-free cascade route to synthesize diarylamines from renewable, biomass- derived starting materials was developed with air oxidized commercial activated carbon (oACair) as the catalyst. When 1-tetralone and aniline were used as substrates, the reaction delivered 71% N-phenyl-1-naphthylamine at 180 °C in 24 h, with Max. TOF of 0.23 h⁻1, and the catalyst maintained good activity over five cycles. The developed protocol was successfully applied to a scope of 10 different diarylamines with good yields, indicating its broad applicability. Reaction kinetic data, combined with DFT computations, indicate that the functional groups on the carbon material surface involve in both the cascade steps: acidic sites promote imine/enamine formation, whereas quinoidic groups mediate the oxidative dehydrogenation (ODH) step. The unpaired electron spin characteristics of the carbon surface was analyzed with superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) magnetometry and was confirmed involved in the catalyst regeneration by O2, while its extensive porosity was found to be crucial for cleaning the active sites.

abstract: The water-gas shift (WGS) reaction is a key process for industrial hydrogen production used in ammonia synthesis, where Cu–Zn–Al (CZA) catalysts are typically employed. Since similar formulations are also used for methanol synthesis, 1 wt.% Cs2O is often added to mitigate its formation as an unwanted side product. However, this addition has recently been suggested to decrease the mechanical strength of the catalyst, particularly during initial reduction, leading to premature failure. In this study, we investigate how gas composition (particularly water content) and pressure affect the structural and chemical evolution of recovered CZA pellets after a typical reduction protocol, using pseudo-in situ X-ray Diffraction Computed Tomography (XRD-CT). We find that high water content (~20 vol.%) combined with increasing Cs₂O loading markedly promotes Cu⁰ crystallite growth, favours formation of Cu₂O, and enhances ZnO sintering. These effects are most severe at the pellet periphery and ultimately compromise mechanical integrity. The results highlight the critical interplay between steam, pressure, and Cs promotion in governing catalyst stability during activation.

abstract: This work presents a highly efficient photocatalytic system for overall water splitting (OWS) based on cubic CaTiO3 (ACTO) modified with reduced graphene oxide (RGO) as a conductive material. Facet-engineering of ACTO creates anisotropic surface properties that promote directional migration of photogenerated electrons and holes, suppressing charge recombination. Surface modification with RGO further enhances charge separation by providing conductive pathways for electrons, stabilizing surface intermediates, and facilitating interfacial electron migration. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that RGO modification induces interfacial charge redistribution in the RGO/ACTO heterojunction with electrons preferentially migrating toward RGO. As a result, the RGO/ACTO composite exhibits remarkable OWS activity, achieving H2 and O2 evolution rates of 18.7 and 8.7 mmol g-1 h-1, respectively, and an apparent quantum yield (AQY) of 32.6% at 257 nm. Mechanistic analysis based on Gibbs free energy calculations of H adsorption (H*) indicates that RGO modulates the surface electronic structure of ACTO, thereby optimizing H* and promoting proton reduction. These results demonstrate that the synergistic effect between facet-engineered ACTO and conductive RGO effectively enhances charge separation and surface reactions, providing insights for the rational design of high-performance photocatalysts for sacrificial-agent-free OWS.

abstract: Asymmetric catalysis underpins pharmaceutical synthesis but is dominated by homogeneousmolecular catalysts that complicate product separation and recycling. Heterogeneousalternatives, including hybrid systems in which molecular catalysts are immobilised on solidsupports, often suffer from diminished activity and poor stability. Here, we use densityfunctional theory and microkinetic modelling to evaluate intrinsically chiral platinum surfacesas a heterogeneous alternative, taking the hydrogenation of hydroxyacetone to 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PD) as a model reaction. On the mirror-image Pt(643)S and Pt(643)ᴿ surfaces,hydroxyacetone chemisorbs at the undercoordinated chiral kink, and the effective transition-state barriers for the two reaction pathways differ by 0.21 eV, favouring S-1,2-PD on Pt(643)S and R-1,2-PD on Pt(643)ᴿ. By contrast, hydroxyacetone is only physisorbed on the achiral Pt(111) terrace and is hydrogenated to a racemic product with a lower effective barrier of 0.75 eV. Microkinetic modelling that accounts for the realistic coexistence of kink and terrace sites identifies an operational window near 500 K and 10⁻² bar in which strong substrate binding at the chiral kink outcompetes the racemic terrace pathway, yielding enantiomeric excesses approaching 99 %. These results establish chiral Pt(643) surfaces as a viable platform for fully heterogeneous asymmetric hydrogenation and motivate experimental verification.

abstract: Pt-Mn catalysts exhibit high performance for propane dehydrogenation (PDH), yet the influence of the support on active site formation remains debated. This study investigates Pt and bimetallic Pt-Mn species on SiO2 and θ-Al₂O₃. Combined TPR, XPS, and XRD analyses reveal accelerated MnOx reduction on SiO2, yielding 1.2-fold higher metallic Mn0 content. DFT calculations demonstrate that Pt-Mn alloying weakens propylene adsorption and increases C–C cleavage barriers without impairing C–H activation. Morphology and stability are critically support-dependent. While SiO2 facilitates selective bimetallic nanoparticles, θ-Al₂O₃ stabilizes highly undercoordinated Pt clusters that promote rapid α-coke formation and five-fold higher total carbon deposition. By optimizing the support and Mn-loading, a catalyst was developed maintaining 98% propylene selectivity over 18 days with an exceptionally low deactivation constant (k_d) of 0.0009 1/h. These insights provide a clear strategy for designing supported bimetallic catalysts with tailored selectivity for hydrocarbon conversion.

abstract: The electronic structure of supported nickel (Ni) single-atom (SA) cocatalysts is governed by interactions with neighboring coordinating atoms, enabling photocatalytic hydrogen evolution activities comparable with those of homogeneous catalysts. Nevertheless, the controlled synthesis of Ni SA catalysts and elucidation of their action mechanisms are significantly challenging. Herein, we report a strategy for confining Ni SAs via oxygen vacancies on a hollow, dandelion-like titanium oxide (TiO 2–x ) support. The Ni–V O –TiO 2–x catalyst exhibited markedly enhanced hydrogen evolution performance, achieving an activity of ∼ 2.6-fold higher than that of oxygen vacancy–free Ni-TiO 2 . Oxygen vacancies on TiO 2–x can function as atomic-scale traps that stabilize isolated Ni atoms, forming Ni SA catalysts with well-defined coordination environments. The reaction mechanism and structure–activity relationship were elucidated by integrating techniques for characterizing oxygen vacancies and SAs with theoretical modeling. Adsorption energy calculations demonstrate that oxygen vacancies on TiO 2 are more favorable for adsorbing Ni SAs than Ni clusters, and electron localization function analysis further reveals significant charge accumulation around Ni SA active centers. This study advances vacancy engineering as a versatile strategy for modulating SA electronic structures and coordination environments, providing a broadly applicable framework for the development of high-performance photocatalysts for hydrogen evolution.

abstract: Ethenolysis, the catalytic cross-metathesis of carbon-carbon double bonds with ethylene, represents an important route for the production of high-value terminal olefins. In this work, density functional theory (DFT) calculations and parallel machine learning (ML) analyses were employed to investigate the factors that alter the reaction selectivity during ruthenium-catalyzed ethenolysis of ethyl oleate. In this context, the selectivity was evaluated as the competition between productive metathesis (PM) and self-metathesis (SM), with the thermodynamic preference for catalyst recovery emerging as the determinant process. In particular, the overall reaction energy associated with PM and, in turn, catalyst regeneration, consistently correlates with experimental selectivity trends. Complementary ML analyses, based on tree-based ensemble algorithms, further demonstrate that catalytic performance arises from multidimensional relationships between various steric and electronic descriptors rather than from isolated electronic properties. These findings establish a predictive framework for the rational design and evaluation of selective ruthenium catalysts for sustainable olefin metathesis applications.

abstract: Competitive and trapping experiments demonstrated that the reductive cyclization of o -nitrobiphenyl to carbazole using CO as the reductant and a palladium/phenanthroline catalyst proceeds through the formation of free o -nitrosobiphenyl. A kinetic study of its cyclization reaction to N -hydroxycarbazole indicated that the reaction does not require a metal catalyst, but is accelerated by bases, as also observed in the catalytic reaction starting from the nitro compound. Theoretical calculations provided details on the mechanism, including the involvement of DMF (solvent), when no additional base is added. The cyclization reaction is similar in the case of the synthesis of indoles from o -nitrostyrenes, but the two reactions show different sensitivities to air. This was attributed to different rate-determining steps, involving a Pd(II) complex as the resting state for the synthesis of carbazoles and a Pd(0) one for that of indoles. A palladacyclic complex was isolated from a reaction of o -nitrobiphenyl under conditions close to those employed in the catalytic reaction and shown to afford carbazole when reacted with pressurized CO. For the synthesis of indoles, a Pd(0) olefin complex, Pd(Phen)(η 2 -(E)-3-(5-fluoro-2-nitrophenyl)-1-phenylprop-2-en-1-one), was isolated directly from a catalytic reaction and characterized by single crystal XRD. An analogous complex, Pd(Phen)(η 2 -methyl ( E )-2-nitrocinnamate), was also independently synthesized and structurally characterized, affording 2-carboxymethyl-indole when treated with CO. Some previously reported pieces of evidence apparently in favor of the involvement of metal-imido species as intermediates in cyclization reactions of nitroarenes when CO is employed as a reductant were dismissed. In particular, a compound previously identified as an aziridine was proven to be an allylic amine, whose formation does not require a metal-imido intermediate. Overall, the results strongly indicate that the cyclization occurs outside the metal coordination sphere at the nitrosoarene stage, excluding the involvement of imido (nitrene) complexes.

abstract: The concept of confinement in zeolite catalysis is invoked to describe dispersive host–guest interactions as facilitated by micropores of molecular dimension. This study extends confinement effects to mesoporous aluminosilicate catalysts in reactions involving (poly)aromatic reactant molecules and transition states that approach relevant mesopore length scales. In alkylation reactions between 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene and dibenzyl ether, which cannot access protons in medium- and small-pore zeolitic micropores, congruent enthalpic and entropic energy barriers were extracted from zeroth order rate constants for MFI and Al-MCM-41. These equivalent reactivities on zeolite crystal surfaces and Al-MCM-41 mesopores for reactants that are “small” relative to proton environments additionally indicate that these protons are of similar acid strength. Contrastingly, nonidentical rates in self-etherification of 1-pyrenemethanol (PM), a tetracyclic primary alcohol, were revealed to result from PM monomer and dimer MASI identities in MFI and Al-MCM-41, respectively, which yielded a difference in their apparent activation energies. The discrepancy in monomer and dimer site coverages was attributed to disfavored dimer formation in Al-MCM-41, as dimers approached Al-MCM-41 pore diameters, whereas MFI external surfaces lacked this confinement-induced restriction. These findings illustrate how rates (and in turn, selectivities) dictated by stabilizing van der Waals in zeolites can be sensitive to such forces in systems as the one presented herein where guest species are comparable in size to their mesoporous containers, potentially affording an additional lever to consider in catalyst design and selection for bulky molecule transformations.

title: Experimental and mechanistic insights on the CO2 hydrogenation to ethanol over KRhFe supported catalysts: a study of support effect
abstract: The effect of the support on the CO 2 hydrogenation to ethanol reaction over KRhFe catalysts supported on different oxides (SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 , TiO 2 , TiO 2 -ZrO 2 , and SiO 2 -Al 2 O 3 ) was investigated through a multi-technique approach combining catalytic tests with extensive physicochemical characterisation, including XAS and operando DRIFTS-MS. H 2 -TPR, TEM and XAS analyses revealed that non-reducible supports, such as SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 , stabilise partially oxidised, well-dispersed Rh and Fe species, while maintaining moderate Rh–Fe interactions. In contrast, reducible supports like TiO 2 and TiO 2 -ZrO 2 facilitate the reduction of RhO x and FeO x species. This translates into markedly different catalytic behaviours: SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 -supported catalysts exhibited enhanced selectivity towards ethanol, whereas TiO 2 and TiO 2 -ZrO 2 -supported catalysts showed higher CO 2 conversion, predominantly yielding CO and CH 4 . Operando DRIFTS-MS results further revealed plausible support-dependent surface intermediates and reaction pathways. The SiO 2 -supported catalyst appears to mainly follow a CO-mediated pathway, while the Al 2 O 3 -supported catalyst exhibited intense formate-related features, suggesting the participation of formate/methoxy intermediates in oxygenate formation. In contrast, TiO 2 promoted RWGS and methanation reactions, limiting C–C coupling. Finally, the incorporation of ZrO 2 into the support (TiO 2 -ZrO 2 ) improved the formation of oxygenates compared to TiO 2 alone, likely due to enhanced stabilisation of adsorbed CO species and their coupling with methoxy intermediates. Overall, these results underscore the critical role of metal–support interactions in governing the selectivity between C1 products and oxygenates during high-pressure CO 2 hydrogenation.

Insights into the active Fe species of Fe/ZSM-5 catalysts for ethane dehydrogenation
abstract: Catalytic ethane dehydrogenation to ethylene is an attractive route for ethylene production following the shale gas revolution. However, its industrial implementation remains challenging due to high costs and environmental concerns. Iron-based catalysts have been identified as promising alternatives, while their catalytic performance is significantly dependent on the coordination environment and oxidation state of the iron species. Herein, a series of Fe/ZSM-5 catalysts were synthesized via urea precipitation (FeZ-P) and incipient wetness impregnation (FeZ-I) methods to investigate the relationship between Fe species evolution and catalytic behavior during ethane dehydrogenation. The FeZ-P catalysts exhibited significantly enhanced activity compared with FeZ-I, which was attributed to the improved dispersion of iron species and their favorable transformation behavior under reaction conditions. Detailed characterizations of fresh and spent catalysts revealed that the initial Fe2O3 species on FeZ-P surface possessed limited dehydrogenation activity but underwent reaction-induced reduction and carbonization, generating Fe3C with enhanced ethane dehydrogenation performance. In contrast, the Fe2O3 bulks on FeZ-I exhibited slower transformation rates, resulting in inferior catalytic activity. Air oxidation treatment enabled partial regeneration of the catalyst by removing carbon deposits and modifying Fe species evolution. This study highlights the importance of regulating Fe species dispersion and dynamic reduction-carbonization behavior, through which catalytically active Fe3C can be generated for enhanced ethane dehydrogenation performance. These findings provide valuable insights into the rational design of efficient Fe-based catalysts for non-oxidative alkane dehydrogenation.

A systematic study of CO methylation by surface methoxy species in different zeolites
abstract: Ketene chemistry is a topic of continuous investigation in zeolite catalysis, as it is key to carbon valorization processes towards high value hydrocarbons. Ketene formation typically occurs through CO methylation by a surface methoxy species (SMS) formed at Brønsted acid sites of zeolites. Here, we present a systematic study of SMS carbonylation reactions on all the possible active sites of six of the most commonly used zeolite frameworks: MOR, FER, CHA, MFI, Beta polymorph A (BEA), and FAU. Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the PBE-D3 functional with single point calculations with the ω B97M-D4 functional. The lowest Gibbs free energy barrier obtained for CO methylation by an SMS is 143 kJ mol −1 at the most favorable site of both MFI and MOR zeolites. For MOR, this is the well-known position in the side pocket, which allows for a favorable positioning of the transition state with a high dispersion contribution from the surrounding framework. On FER and BEA zeolites, comparable sites do not exist, and thus higher free energy barriers were obtained. The CHA and FAU zeolites, which present large cavities, showed the highest barriers, indicating their lower activity for this reaction, compared to other reactions with larger molecules. The results were compared to those obtained experimentally, with an overall good agreement in terms of carbonylation rates

Atomic-thick two-dimensional Janus interphase catalyst with an interfacial ionic liquid bridge for quasi-homogeneous Pickering interfacial catalysis
abstract: Pickering emulsions are of considerable interest in the chemical industry because they provide large oil–water interfacial areas for interfacial catalysis. However, solid emulsifiers located at oil–water interface often impede the mass transfer across the interface, thereby limiting the reactivity of biphasic reactions. Here we report a quasi-homogeneous Pickering interfacial catalysis strategy to overcome this diffusion barrier by employing an ultrathin amphiphilic Janus film as the solid emulsifier and introducing a compatible ionic liquid (IL) as a multifunctional interfacial bridge. Hydrophobic chiral neat TiIV salen complexes (Ti(salen)) were thus selectively grafted onto one side of single-layer porous graphene oxide (PGO) through an imidazolium-based IL linker, enabling asymmetric oxidation of sulfides with H₂O₂ in water. The atomic-thick GO film precisely positions Ti(salen) catalytic sites at oil–water interface, while the hydrophilic IL moieties located on the hydrophobic catalytic side acts as molecular bridge between the oil and aqueous phases owing to their unique compatibility. This engineered interfacial microenvironment allows the water-soluble oxidant to directly access the hydrophobic substrate at the catalytic interface without a significant diffusion barrier. As a consequence, asymmetric sulfoxidation in water proceeds in a quasi-homogeneous manner, affording a broad range of chiral sulfoxides in excellent yields (93–98%) and enantioselectivities (92–99% ee), surpassing the performance of most reported Pickering interfacial catalysts. Moreover, the quasi-homogeneous Pickering interfacial catalysis strategy also delivers efficient asymmetric sulfa-Michael addition in water when chiral FeⅢ–salen complexes are used as catalytic sites.

Internal transport modulates catalytic hydrogenolysis of polyolefins
abstract: Catalytic hydrogenolysis offers a route to selectively upcycle plastics into fuel-range hydrocarbons, but internal diffusion limitations in porous catalysts can restrict polymer access to active sites and promote secondary hydrogenolysis reactions. This work investigates how the spatial distribution of Ru active sites influences hydrogenolysis of hexadecane (C16), octacosane (C28), and LDPE (~4 kDa, >C200). Ru/SiO₂ catalysts with similar Ru particle sizes (~14 nm) but different active-site spatial distribution were compared: an internal/external-site catalyst, with Ru distributed throughout the pores and external surface, and an external-site catalyst, with Ru located exclusively on the external surface. For C16, site-normalized rates and product distributions were unaffected by catalyst-support particle size or site distribution, with a Weisz–Prater criterion of ~0.02, indicating negligible internal diffusion limitations. In contrast, C28 and LDPE showed strong transport limitations on the internal/external-site catalyst, with decreasing rates as support particle size increased and increasing formation of C1-C4 products. The external-site catalyst gave substantially higher rates, two times higher yield to liquid-range products for C28, and five times higher liquid yields for LDPE. These results show that restricting active sites to the external surface improves active-site utilization, suppresses secondary hydrogenolysis, and enhances liquid hydrocarbon yields for high-molecular-weight substrates.

Activation barriers in the glycolysis of PET as catalyzed by tertiary amines: Density functional calculations and predictions from interpretable machine learning
abstract: The efficient chemical recycling of poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is a crucial part of any sustainable circular plastic economy. The depolymerization of PET can take place via a glycolysis reaction with tertiary amines as catalysts. We investigate this reaction using density functional calculations with the M06-L functional, complemented by interpretable machine learning. A PET dimer containing C–O linkages is used as a representative model of the active region or the polymer. The concerted and the stepwise mechanisms of its glycolysis using trimethylamine as a catalyst are examined. The calculations reveal that the reaction proceeds preferentially via a stepwise mechanism with which the proton abstraction process being the rate-determining step. The structure–activity relationship shows that, in general, amines with side chains that are better electron donors enhance the reactivity. Deviations from this trend can be attributed to steric hindrance and resonance effects. Based on the analysis of DFT-derived descriptors, the protonation free energy of the tertiary amines is identified as the most important single descriptor for predicting activation barriers. The Sure Independence Screening and Sparsifying Operator (SISSO) method is then employed to develop a few low-dimensional descriptors that enable a reliable prediction of activation barriers based solely on amine properties, thus eliminating the need for the computationally costly explicit transition state calculations.

title: Manganese-catalyzed [2+2+2] cycloaddition reactions – defined precatalyst vs. in situ activation approaches
abstract: The applicability of the cyclopentadienyl oligoolefin manganese complex [Cp’Mn(CHT)] (Cp’ = methylcyclopentadienyl, CHT = η 6 -cycloheptatriene) ( Mn2 ) for the [2 + 2 + 2] cyclotrimerization of triynes to arenes under photochemical conditions is showcased. The reactivity of Mn2 , which is prepared from the commercially available manganese precursor methylcymantrene [Cp’Mn(CO) 3 ] ( Mn1 ) and cycloheptatriene, is demonstrated either as an isolated precatalyst or in an in situ protocol, combining the Mn2 synthesis with the catalytic [2 + 2 + 2] cyclization. The optimization of the reaction conditions as well as the scope and limitation for the cyclotrimerization reaction are outlined. Mechanistically, the reaction is investigated by light-on/light-off experiments and additive/poisoning studies, highlighting the necessity of continuous irradiation and indicating an inner-sphere mechanism.

abstract: Stereodefined ( Z – or E –) alkenes are essential organic functionalities in organic chemistry, either as intermediate or final products, and their synthesis heavily relies in the stereoselective hydrogenation of internal alkynes. Here we show that the one–pot internal alkyne formation (via Sonogashira reaction) / selective semi–hydrogenation reaction with H 2 to give the Z alkene / isomerization reaction to give the E alkene is catalyzed by Pd and iodide (eventually added as PdI 2 and an additional iodide source) without the need of any ligand, copper co–catalyst, organic hydride source or solid support. This simple procedure is based on the concomitant action of catalytic Pd and I atoms during the different events of the reaction sequence, leveraging the iodide atoms produced as a by–product during the first Sonogashira reaction for a selective semi-hydrogenation reaction and allowing an isomerization after the simple addition of an iodide source. In this way, the desired Z – or E –alkenes are obtained at wish by simple denying or not the evolution of the last isomerization reaction step. Machine–learning workflows and a technoeconomic analysis confirm the removal of all the unnecessary reagents as a natural evolution of this cascade reaction, to be simply catalyzed by a Pd salt.

abstract: Platinum is widely used as a promoter for cobalt-based Fischer–Tropsch catalysts to improve the degree of reduction, but the extent to which impregnation sequence and deposition chemistry govern platinum distribution and promotion behaviour has not been evaluated systematically. Here, Pt-Co/SiO 2 catalysts containing ∼10 wt-% Co and 0.05 wt-% Pt were prepared by sequential impregnation on a pre-calcined Co/SiO 2 catalyst using either an aqueous H 2 PtCl 6 -solution at pH = 2 or an aqueous Pt(NH 3 ) 4 Cl 2 −solution at an initial pH = 9 and compared to a co-impregnated and an unpromoted catalyst. Control experiments showed preferential adsorption of platinum on Co 3 O 4 at pH = 2 and on SiO 2 at pH = 9. Acidic control experiments showed more leaching of cobalt and silica from Co 3 O 4 /SiO 2 relative to pure Co 3 O 4 and SiO 2 . The reducibility of cobalt was improved almost independent of the method of deposition possibly implying that the formation of the difficult to reduce cobalt species is formed during the reduction process. Under Fischer–Tropsch conditions, sequentially impregnated platinum at pH = 9 exhibited the highest initial cobalt-time yield (CTY 0 ), consistent with its superior metal surface area. Despite a lower dispersion than the unpromoted catalyst, sequentially impregnated platinum at pH = 2 displayed the highest initial turnover frequency (TOF 0 ), suggesting that Pt on or in the cobalt surface enhances intrinsic activity. The second-order deactivation constants (k d ) for the sequentially impregnated catalysts were lower than the co-impregnated catalyst, suggesting that platinum location and distribution influence catalyst stability. Sequential impregnation of platinum increased C 5 + selectivity relative to the co-impregnated and unpromoted catalysts.

Temporal evolution of potential oscillations during ethanol electro-oxidation driven by CHx accumulation: insights from microkinetic modeling
abstract: The ethanol oxidation reaction is outstanding for electrochemical energy conversion devices, which are pivotal for overcoming the challenges of the energy transition. Therefore, it is extremely important to understand the phenomena that govern the reaction kinetics to improve the performance of these devices. In this regard, using microkinetic models alongside experiments under oscillatory conditions has proven to be a promising approach. This study proposes a microkinetic model to elucidate the oscillatory dynamics of ethanol electro-oxidation on platinum in acidic medium by comparing experimental galvanostatic data with computational simulations. By combining 9 reaction steps, the model reproduces the time-dependent potential oscillations, whose main waveform is determined by the dynamics of the surface coverage; specifically, by the competitive adsorption of intermediate species such as O H a d and carbonaceous species, such as, C O a d and C H 3 C O a d . The simulated potential profile reflects key dynamic characteristics that are consistent with experimental observations, showing a progressive increase in period and amplitude. This behavior results from the accumulation of C H x (up to 60 % surface coverage), which prevents the regeneration of active sites. In turn, this accumulation is a consequence of a high selectivity toward partial oxidation products (acetaldehyde and acetic acid), attributed to kinetically favorable pathways that prevent the breaking of the C - C bond. These findings shed light on the reaction mechanisms and lay the groundwork for future simulations under both oscillatory and non-oscillatory conditions, with the aim of improving the catalytic activity of the process.
